newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon, Kuwait, Egypt to cross-trade equities.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon, Kuwait, Egypt to cross-trade equities.

text.p: Cross-trading of equities listed in Lebanon, Egypt and Kuwait will start at the beginning of January under an agreement due to be signed by 80 brokers on Friday, Arab bourse officials said.
The pact, to be signed at a meeting organised by the Union of Arab Stock Exchanges, would effectively bypass the unresolved issue of cross-listing of shares between the three bourses.
"The pact's implementation will be in the first week of January," Sa'faq al-Rukeibi, secretary-general of the Union of Arab Stock Exchanges, said.

"Cross-listing of shares will no longer be an obstacle after the signing of the agreement. Why? Because any broker in his home country, say a Kuwaiti, can fully invest in the Lebanese market or the Egyptian markets," he told Reuters.
Friday's pact follows two earlier pacts among the exchanges and their clearance houses.

In September, the three exchanges signed a deal in Beirut to begin cross-trading of shares next year. In its first stage, the deal guarantees a free flow of updated information to investors and dealers in the three markets.

In October, a co-operation agreement was signed in Cairo between the companies which handle clearing and settlement for the three exchanges -- Misr Clearing Co of Egypt, Midclear of Lebanon and the Kuwaiti Clearing Co.
However, bourse officials and brokers at the Beirut meeting said cross-listing was still down the road, mainly because of the lack of common listing criteria.
"In Beirut bourse we are more open. We don't have restrictions and Egypt is also open. Kuwait still has some restrictions," Gabriel Sehnaoui, Chairman of the Beirut Stock Exchange said.
"To have cross-listing in all the companies, you need to have the same criteria. It needs time," Sehnaoui added.

Rukeibi said Kuwaiti authorities were working on opening up their market to non-Kuwaiti investors for direct share ownership but the process needed time because it would have to be approved by the relevant government institutions.
"At present this can be bypassed in an indirect way, as there are investment funds or managed portfolios in which foreigners can own units," Rukeibi said.

Ziad Makawi, of Beirut-based Middle East Capital Group, said: "The idea is to move to an integrated regional equity market..but I think cross-listing is still a little bit down the road, though these things tend to move in leaps."
The market capitalisation of the Egyptian exchange is $10.5 billion and the Kuwait bourse's is $18 billion.
The Beirut Stock Exchange, which re-opened in January after a shutdown of nearly 13 years, currently lists five industrial companies with a total capitalisation of about $2.4 billion.
